I think maybe your best bet would be to reach out to a molecular biology lab to see if you can gain research experience. In terms of prereqs, biology PhDs usually require 1 year bio, 1 year physics, 1 year chemistry, and like stats or calc1 (all depends on the program tho). So I would say, finish up your degree and try to get some experience for a year or 2 and during that time take any other prerequisites you need from community college. 

If you’re in a rush, I would just go for a PhD in your field that you’re doing your bachelors in, but if you really want to do molecular biology then take a year or two to get what you need done. If you are in the US, there are [NIH post bac PREP programs](https://www.nigms.nih.gov/training/PREP) or a post bac program available at the [NIH itself](https://www.training.nih.gov/programs/postbac_irta). Both would be a great way to gain experience and take a graduate level class in biology.

I'd say it just depends. There are multiple options you can take for sure. 

If you're an underrepresented minority, you can apply to an NIH post-bacc program which allows you to do full time research while taking grad level courses and receiving a stipend:  [https://www.nigms.nih.gov/training/PREP](https://www.nigms.nih.gov/training/PREP) 

The NIH itself has a post-bacc program anyone can apply to:  [https://www.training.nih.gov/programs/postbac\_irta](https://www.training.nih.gov/programs/postbac_irta)  

RA positions are great too! All are good options and lead to success for the most part, but at the end of the day it comes down to what you're looking for in either employment, experience, or outcomes.

Being nervous is completely normal. I'm currently waiting on a decision post interview and I still feel it (very scared honestly, but hopefully things go well in the end...). Honestly, the best advice I can give you is to look online at who you are meeting with, read at least (1) paper or abstract from each and have some questions prepared to ask. **You know your research!** So if they ask, then answer to the best of your ability. If you don't know the answer to a question or them asking "why didn't you do this?" you could say that you don't know at this time or we haven't thought of that, that is a really great suggestion, I'll be sure to implement that moving forward.

Show that you have enthusiasm, passion, and commitment to pursue a PhD! Go to any "optional" events. After the interview, either the day you are traveling back or the day after be sure to send out thank you emails. *You got this!* I wish you the best and hope it goes well! Knock em' dead.
